items.title: Reading a meniscus from the wrong angle changes the answer
items.claim: Read a burette with your eye above the meniscus: you see a high reading. Read with your eye below: a low reading. The error can be several percent — purely from where you put your head.
items.prompt: What's the right way to take the reading?

options.text: Eye level with the meniscus, viewing perpendicular to the scale, so the line of sight passes through the bottom of the meniscus and the scale at the same level
From slightly above to see the bottom of the meniscus better
From below to avoid disturbing the liquid

items.reveal:
Parallax error happens when the object you are reading and the scale you are reading against are at different distances from your eye. Any tilt in viewing angle shifts the apparent position of one relative to the other.

For a meniscus in a burette: the liquid surface and the scale on the burette tube are separated by a few millimetres. Looking down or up at an angle moves them apparently relative to each other.

Same problem with ammeters and voltmeters with mirror scales: align your eye so the needle and its reflection in the mirror coincide. This way you know you're looking perpendicular.

Digital readouts eliminate parallax (the reading is a single number). They introduce other concerns: rounding, response time, calibration drift.
items.why: Lab errors are taught as 'be careful'. Parallax is a specific systematic error with a specific fix — eye level, perpendicular sighting.

items.title: Every measurement in a working lab traces back to seven international standards
items.claim: Every length, mass, temperature, current, time, light intensity and amount of substance measurement at any modern lab can be traced through calibration chains back to seven defined units maintained by international bodies. Calibration is what makes measurements comparable across labs.
items.prompt: What does 'traceable' mean for a measurement?

options.text: The instrument was calibrated against a reference standard, which itself was calibrated against a higher-tier standard, all the way back to the SI definition. Every step has a documented uncertainty
The instrument has a serial number
The measurement was published in a journal

items.reveal_title: Traceability chains and the redefined SI
items.reveal:
In 2019 the SI was redefined so all seven base units are now derived from fundamental constants: the speed of light defines the metre, the Planck constant defines the kilogram (since 2019, replacing the platinum-iridium reference cylinder), the Boltzmann constant defines the kelvin, and so on.

A national metrology institute (NPL in the UK, NIST in the US) maintains primary realisations of these units. Industry calibration labs are calibrated against these primaries. Working labs send instruments to industry labs for periodic calibration.

When you read a balance display in a school lab, the number you see has a chain of calibration certificates behind it linking it back to the Planck constant via a Kibble balance.
items.why: Calibration is treated as paperwork. It is the substrate that makes any quantitative claim comparable across labs, countries and decades.

items.title: Two metal plates attract through empty space
items.claim: Place two parallel uncharged metal plates a micrometre apart in a vacuum. They attract. The force isn't gravity, isn't electrostatic — it's a measurable consequence of quantum vacuum fluctuations.

options.text: The vacuum supports a sea of fluctuating electromagnetic modes; between the plates only certain wavelengths fit, so the radiation pressure inside is less than outside — net force pushes the plates together
Charge accumulated on the plate surfaces

items.reveal_title: The Casimir effect — radiation pressure from nothing
items.reveal:
Even in 'empty' space, quantum field theory predicts a sea of virtual photons. Between two parallel metal plates, only photons with wavelengths fitting an integer number of half-wavelengths in the gap can exist (a quantisation condition like a particle in a box). Outside the plates, ALL wavelengths exist.

This produces an imbalance in vacuum-radiation pressure. The plates feel more 'push' from outside than from inside, and so are pushed together.

The force is tiny: about 1.3 millionths of a newton per square metre at 1 micrometre separation. Lamoreaux measured it in 1997, confirming Casimir's 1948 prediction. The vacuum is not nothing.
items.why: The classical vacuum is empty. The quantum vacuum is full of fluctuating fields that have measurable mechanical consequences.
